It does not stop tagging. It changes what tagging costs.

A coated wall still gets hit. What changes is that the aerosol lands on a barrier instead of in the masonry, so removal becomes a wash rather than a chemical job with a ghost left behind. On a wall that is tagged more than twice a year, the coating usually pays for itself inside twelve months.

  • Removal becomes a wash
  • Usually pays back within a year on a repeat target
  • Honest about walls not worth coating

The arithmetic

On a bare porous wall, every tag is a treatment: solvent, dwell, mechanical work, and on block or unsealed brick a permanent ghost that each subsequent removal makes slightly worse. Four removals a year on a bare wall and the wall is progressively ruined as well as expensive.

On a coated wall, the paint cannot reach the substrate. Removal is water and a mild cleaner, the wall comes back to the same condition every time, and there is no cumulative damage. The coating costs money once. The removals cost money forever. Where a wall is genuinely a repeat target, the decision is straightforward, and where it is not, we will say so.

Sacrificial or permanent

The only real choice to make

Two systems, genuinely different economics.
  Sacrificial Permanent
How it works A wax or polymer layer that comes off with the paint A cured coating that the paint cannot bond to
Removal method Hot water wash, which takes the coating with it Solvent wipe. The coating stays
After a removal The coating has to be reapplied to that area Nothing. It is ready for the next one
Upfront cost Lower Higher
Cost per removal Reapplication each time Essentially just labour
Appearance Usually invisible, sometimes a slight sheen Can add a noticeable sheen on matt surfaces
Service life Until it is used, or a few years of weather Five to ten years depending on the system and exposure
Best for Occasional targets, heritage and porous surfaces Frequent targets where removals are regular

When we would tell you not to bother

A wall that gets tagged once every few years does not need coating, and the money is better spent on removal when it happens. A wall in poor condition should be repaired first, because a coating over failing render or spalling concrete fails with it. And a heritage or unusual masonry surface needs a conservation opinion rather than a product, because some coatings trap moisture in a wall that needs to breathe.

  • Twice a yearRoughly the frequency above which a coating starts making financial sense.
  • No ghostingThe real benefit on porous block and brick, where repeated bare removals leave cumulative shadow.
  • Clean firstA coating goes on a clean surface. Existing tags are removed before anything is applied.
  • 5 to 10 yearsService life of a permanent system, depending on exposure and how often it is cleaned.

Questions

Asked before coating a wall

Will a coating stop my wall being tagged?

No, and nobody should tell you otherwise. It changes what happens afterwards: the paint sits on the coating instead of going into the masonry, so removal is a wash rather than a chemical job and the wall comes back to the same condition every time.

How much does it cost?

Per square metre, with the system and the surface setting the rate. Permanent coatings cost more upfront and less per removal. Sacrificial coatings are cheaper upfront and have to be reapplied where they are used.

The honest comparison is against what you currently spend on removals. We can put both in the quote.

Will it change how the wall looks?

Sacrificial coatings are usually close to invisible. Permanent coatings can add a slight sheen, which is noticeable on a matt surface like unsealed block and barely visible on a surface that already has some gloss.

We can do a test panel so you can see it before committing a whole elevation.

Does the wall have to be cleaned first?

Yes, completely. A coating over an existing tag locks it in permanently, and a coating over a dirty wall does not bond properly.

Existing graffiti is removed first as a separate step. Graffiti removal covers that part.

Can you coat a heritage building?

With a conservation opinion, and not on our say so. Some coatings trap moisture in masonry that needs to breathe, and on a heritage wall that is a serious problem.

Where a building is listed or the masonry is unusual, the right sequence is a heritage consultant first and a product decision second.

How long does it last?

A permanent system, five to ten years depending on exposure and how often it is cleaned. A sacrificial system lasts until it is used, plus whatever weathering takes off it, and is reapplied to the areas that have been cleaned.

Frequency is the whole decision. Everything else follows from it.

  1. How often it is taggedOnce a year, four times, monthly. This decides whether a coating is worth it at all.
  2. What the wall isBlock, brick, render, precast or painted, and roughly the area.
